paras: The killing of Abram Hardy took place on August 30, 1915, in Newberry County, South Carolina, when three officers shot Hardy, a Black man of about 40, while trying to arrest him near his home. A coroner's jury found that day that they had acted in the discharge of their duties, and they were released on bail. The Newberry Herald and News printed the inquest testimony in full under the headline "Preferred Death to Being Arrested."

According to the Newberry paper, Magistrate J. Alonzo Kinard had issued a warrant several days earlier charging Hardy with disorderly conduct and cursing on the public highway. The Yorkville Enquirer gave a different ground, saying Hardy had refused to pay his street tax and to work the streets in place of it. Early on the morning of August 30, Kinard and his constable, H. B. Richardson, went to arrest Hardy, who refused to go and, by Kinard's account, said he would die before he would be arrested.
Kinard telephoned Sheriff C. G. Blease for help at about 10 o'clock. Blease sent Deputy Sheriff William M. Dorroh, deputized J. H. Chappell to go with him, and had J. R. Workman drive the car.

Joined by Kinard, the officers reached Hardy's house, where his wife, Carrie Hardy, said he had walked off toward a patch of pines. Hardy came out of the pines carrying a hickory stick and an old axe handle, and the three men went out to meet him.

In the officers' sworn accounts, Dorroh told Hardy he had a warrant and ordered him to drop the sticks, and Hardy refused and came at them. Dorroh said Hardy swung at him, after which Dorroh shot him in the leg and then in the breast while Chappell also fired. Hardy then knocked Kinard down with a blow to the head, and the officers kept firing, Kinard joining in once he got up. The Herald and News said it took six shots to stop him, and a doctor found pistol wounds in his thigh, shoulder, breast, neck and head.

His wife and his daughter Daisy said they turned away as the shooting began, and both said he had told them that morning he would not be with them long. B. I. Sease testified that he saw Hardy run up on the officers and scuffle with them, and had heard him say he would not be arrested.

The sheriff and coroner went to the scene, where a coroner's jury of six heard the testimony. The jury found that Hardy died of gunshot wounds at the hands of Dorroh, Chappell and Kinard "while acting in the discharge of their duties as peace officers."

Blease arrested the three men "under the law" and took them to jail, and that evening their attorneys obtained bail from Associate Justice Watts at Laurens. The Laurens Advertiser put the bail at $500 each, which the Newberry paper called "nominal sums." The officers were to appear before the grand jury at the next term of court, but no report of grand jury action or a trial was found.

The Newberry Herald and News gave the story and the testimony much of its August 31 front page. Its headlines, "Preferred Death to Being Arrested" and "Negro Shot By Officers Discharging Their Duty," took the officers' side, and its account described the "unpleasant duty" of men "forced to kill" Hardy. It also said Hardy had a "rather bad reputation," was said to have been "crazed from the use of cocaine," and had recently left the state asylum, claims absent from the sworn testimony it printed.

On September 1 the Laurens Advertiser reported the bail hearing and said, with a hedge, that Hardy "it appears, had resisted arrest." On September 3 the Yorkville Enquirer gave it one paragraph in its "Palmetto Gleanings" column of state news and tied the arrest to unpaid street tax.

The papers disagree on why Hardy was being arrested: the Newberry paper, drawing on the inquest, cited a warrant for disorderly conduct and cursing, while the Yorkville Enquirer cited unpaid street tax. Every account of the fight comes from the three men who shot Hardy and from Sease.

reader.title: Killing of Abram Hardy
bases: A deputy sheriff, a specially deputized man and a magistrate shot and killed Abram Hardy while trying to arrest him on a warrant; no crowd or mob is reported (A2, A3, A1).

The Newberry paper's inquest record (A1, A2, A3), a Laurens report of the officers' bail hearing (A4) and a Yorkville state-news item (A5) agree that the three officers shot and killed Hardy while trying to arrest him, though the account of the fight comes only from the officers and one witness.

accounts.label: Officers' sworn testimony
accounts.gist: Kinard, Chappell and Dorroh swore that Hardy came at them with a hickory stick and an axe handle, refused to drop them, swung at Dorroh and knocked Kinard down, and kept fighting until repeated shots brought him down.

accounts.label: Family and neighbor testimony
accounts.gist: Hardy's wife and daughter said he had told them he would not be with them long and that they turned away as the shooting started; B. I. Sease said he saw Hardy run up on the officers and scuffle, and had heard him say he would not be arrested.

accounts.label: Newberry editor's narrative
accounts.gist: The Herald and News said the officers were 'forced to kill' Hardy, added that he was said to use cocaine and had been released from the asylum, and suggested he was trying to reach a shotgun at his house.

accounts.label: Yorkville state-news item
accounts.gist: Said Hardy was sought for refusing to pay his street tax or work the streets, struck the officers with a stick and was then shot and killed.

framing.detail: The Herald and News headlined 'Preferred Death to Being Arrested' and 'Negro Shot By Officers Discharging Their Duty', called Hardy a 'negro of rather bad reputation' said to be 'crazed from the use of cocaine', and described the officers' 'unpleasant duty' of being 'forced to kill' him.
The Laurens Advertiser reported only the bail hearing, with the hedge that Hardy 'it appears, had resisted arrest'.
The Yorkville Enquirer gave the killing one paragraph in its state roundup and tied the arrest to unpaid street tax.

versions.value: Warrant for disorderly conduct and cursing on the public highway, issued by Magistrate Kinard several days earlier
Refusal to pay his street tax and to work the streets in lieu of it

conflicts.note: The Newberry paper is local and drew on the inquest, where Kinard testified a warrant had been issued before him; the Yorkville item is a secondhand state roundup. The two may not exclude each other, but the papers give different grounds.

versions.value: Dorroh and Chappell, joined by Kinard
Dorroh, Chappell and Workman (Dorroh's testimony); Blease said he deputized Workman to drive the car

conflicts.note: All accounts agree the three who fired were Dorroh, Chappell and Kinard; Workman appears only as the driver.
Not contradictory; the Laurens paper gives the figure.

info: Monday, August 30, 1915, in the morning (the Newberry paper of Aug. 31 says 'yesterday'; the inquest documents are dated Aug. 30, 1915)
At and near Abram Hardy's house in No. 10 township, Newberry County; Hardy was met crossing a cotton patch after coming out of a patch of pines
Abram Hardy, described as a 'negro' about 40 years old; Kinard put him at about 220 pounds and six feet tall

Charged on a magistrate's warrant with disorderly conduct and cursing on the public highway (Newberry paper); the Yorkville Enquirer instead said he had refused to pay his street tax and to work the streets in lieu of it

Associate Justice Watts at Laurens granted the three bail, in 'nominal sums' (Newberry) or $500 each (Laurens); they were to appear before the grand jury at the next term of court. No report of grand jury action or a trial was found.
